Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) may have limited usefulness in differentiating unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS) from minimally conscious state (MCS) patients. While tDCS has been shown to be effective in improving motor function and behavior in MCS patients, its utility in distinguishing between UWS and MCS is unclear.

In unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, patients typically lack purposeful behavior due to severe impairment of brainstem functions, which may not respond to stimulation. In contrast, minimally conscious state patients are characterized by some level of consciousness and ability to react to stimuli, but their primary issue lies in the degree of reduced cortical activity rather than impaired motor function.

While tDCS can be effective in MCS patients, its ability to differentiate between UWS and MCS is not well established. In fact, one study found that tDCS had no significant effect on predicting further course in patients with wakefulness state who displayed residual connectivity markers (indicative of some level of cortical activity). This suggests that tDCS may not be a reliable tool for distinguishing between these two states.

Therefore, while tDCS has potential benefits in improving motor function and behavior in MCS patients, its utility in differentiating unresponsive wakefulness syndrome from minimally conscious state patients is limited. Other factors, such as clinical evaluation and imaging studies (e.g., EEG), may be necessary to make an accurate diagnosis.
